8b97 Approach: 'CompletionAgentStep records the caught exception's .diagnostic onto self.failure_diagnostic when it enters recovery (fd84 adds the budget entry edge; this ticket makes the diagnostic it carries survive)'

findings.finding: Making per-run usage recording default-on is a behavior change (previously not durable-by-default) but the plan does not acknowledge its storage/write-cost footprint on every gate run nor offer a back-out (e.g. a disable switch) if the durable recording proves costly at scale.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State in the Approach how the runaway trip sequences the two named mechanisms: does it steer (synthetic tool results) for N steps first and raise the typed runaway error into bounded recovery only if steering fails to land, and is recovery therefore the fallback rather than the first response?
evidence: Parent Approach: 'a typed runaway error classified ahead of the provider-outage fallback in interpret_failure, routed into the shipped bounded recovery + tool-free finalizer'
Child c827 proposal comment: 'ESCALATION LADDER: steer for N steps (propose N=6). If the model still will not land, raise a NEW typed exception ToolLoopDetected'
e1b1 Approach: steering is the forced-landing primitive; the typed-error-into-recovery path is a distinct downstream stage

The parent separately names both the steering toolset (criterion 2) and the typed runaway error (criterion 1) without stating that the steering stage precedes and gates the typed-error stage on the same trip signal
findings.finding: The parent Approach presents the runaway actuator as a single leg ('a typed runaway error classified ahead of the provider-outage fallback ... routed into the shipped bounded recovery'), but the reconciled child design (c827) is a two-stage escalation ladder: steer with synthetic tool results for N steps first, and raise the typed error into recovery only if the model still will not land. The parent's summary omits the steer-first stage and does not state whether recovery runs on every trip or only after steering fails -- the trip-to-recover sequencing is left under-reconciled at the parent level even though it determines the common-case control flow.
findings.location: Plan 'Approach' paragraph (sentence beginning 'Then wire the detector to ACT during the run')
scenarios: An implementer reading only the parent could wire the trip to raise the typed error immediately (skipping the steering stage the parent independently mandates for the forced landing), or wire steering without connecting it to the runaway trip -- two mechanisms sharing one detector signal but with unstated ordering
findings.suggested_fix: Add one clause to the Approach making the ladder explicit at the parent level, e.g. 'a detected runaway first steers the model to land via synthetic tool results (the same primitive replacing the empty-filter cutoff); only if it will not land within N steps does a typed runaway error route into bounded recovery + the tool-free finalizer.'

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Add a one-line prior-art reference for the windowed distinct-ratio stuck detector (e.g. OpenHands StuckDetector, AutoGPT looping heuristics) and the synthetic-tool-result steering pattern, confirming the window/trip choice is calibrated against known detectors rather than only the two local traces.

findings.location: Approach / Child decomposition (detector signal `distinct_ratio_window`; steering toolset)
scenarios: Threshold/window values (24, 0.50) chosen without cross-checking how comparable stuck detectors size their windows and trip points
Synthetic-tool-result steering re-derived from scratch when framework/community patterns already exist

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Specify the synthetic tool result's steering text/vocabulary the model reads at the tool-step boundary (e.g. that the tool budget is spent, that further calls return the same steer, and to summarize/land now) so the executor authors it from the plan, not from guesswork.
evidence: Plan: 'the tool_step_limit empty-filter rewrite ... keep tools advertised and steer with synthetic tool results instead.'

A synthetic tool result is a string the model reads and is expected to act on (land / stop calling), i.e. an LLM-facing instruction — but the plan never states its wording or the value vocabulary (e.g. a stop directive, the fact that the limit was reached, that further calls will be refused).
No existing steering-message constant exists in the tree (searched 'steer'/'synthetic' — only unrelated hits), so the executor cannot recover the text from the codebase.
T8(a): a protocol/instruction referenced but whose content vocabulary is never defined.
findings.finding: The synthetic-tool-result steering primitive is an LLM-consumed instruction whose text/vocabulary is never defined in the plan.
findings.location: Approach paragraph ('keep tools advertised and steer with synthetic tool results instead'); Child decomposition ('the protocol-safe forced landing (steering toolset replacing the empty-filter cutoff)')
scenarios: The executor must author the steering-result text and, absent a spec, may write a message the model ignores or misreads, silently defeating the forced-landing that criterion 2 depends on.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Name the terminal bound for a model that keeps calling tools after being steered (e.g. eff_max_iter / UsageLimitExceeded routed into the actuator's bounded recovery) and state the resulting verdict outcome.
evidence: Plan keeps tool definitions advertised for the whole run by design ('keep tools advertised'), so a non-cooperative model is free to re-issue tool calls and receive the same steered result each time.

The plan states no terminal bound for a model that never voluntarily lands after being steered; the existing backstop (interpret_failure's UsageLimitExceeded arm, structured_run.py:75) is never co-located as that fallback.
T8(d): an unspecified fallback for an incomplete/failed sub-step (the model never completing the 'land now' step).
findings.finding: The plan does not specify the fallback when a steered model keeps calling tools instead of landing.
findings.location: Approach paragraph (steering toolset / forced landing); AC line 2
scenarios: A model that treats each steered tool result as a transient error and re-issues calls, consuming the full step budget and re-surfacing as an exhaustion — the very failure this work targets — with no named landing bound.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] State the runaway classification's exact position in interpret_failure's ordered isinstance dispatch relative to the existing UsageLimitExceeded arm (before it, or as a refinement inside it), given that a runaway manifests as a step-budget exhaustion.
evidence: Plan places the new classification 'ahead of the provider-outage fallback', but a runaway is itself a step-budget exhaustion whose current handler is the UsageLimitExceeded arm raised FIRST in interpret_failure (confirmed structured_run.py:75, order: UsageLimitExceeded -> LLMError -> sampling -> provider-outage).

'Ahead of the provider-outage fallback' does not disambiguate whether the runaway branch runs BEFORE or replaces the UsageLimitExceeded arm — the arm that already produces the LLMRunnerError with the repetition diagnostic.
T8(c)-adjacent: a decision-rule/branch whose placement in an ordered isinstance dispatch is ambiguous, and the order 'IS the contract' per the module docstring.
findings.finding: The runaway classification's placement relative to interpret_failure's existing UsageLimitExceeded arm is ambiguous.
findings.location: Approach paragraph ('a typed runaway error classified ahead of the provider-outage fallback in interpret_failure')
scenarios: An implementer inserts the runaway branch after the UsageLimitExceeded arm, where the exhaustion has already been re-raised as LLMRunnerError, so the runaway is never classified and never routed to bounded recovery — criterion 1 silently unmet.
